title: Continuous Chain of Thought Enables Parallel Exploration
one_liner: Instead of picking one word at a time, a language model can generate soft blends of many words at once, letting it explore multiple reasoning paths in parallel.
lead: Language models normally think step by step by picking one word from a list and then the next word and so on. This paper asks: what if the model could generate a soft blend of many words at each step instead of just one? That blend gives the model room to track multiple reasoning branches at the same time, like exploring several paths through a maze without committing to one choice until the end.

problem.h2: Why picking one word at a time gets stuck
paras: Today's language models solve reasoning problems by thinking out loud, step by step: they pick the first word, then pick the second, then the third. At each fork in the reasoning path, the model commits to one choice and keeps going. If that choice was wrong, it is too late to switch.

A beginner might hope the model could just try several paths at once, like exploring multiple ideas at the same time. But the model's normal word-picking process does not allow that. Each step locks in one discrete choice from the vocabulary, and there is no room to hold multiple possibilities in parallel. Some reasoning problems, like finding the minimum sum of a set of numbers, need the model to track many branches at once to avoid dead ends.

callout.html: Standard models pick one word at each step, so they cannot explore multiple reasoning paths in parallel.

The model tracks all outcomes together and picks the best one.
During training, teach the model to output the right mixture weights by showing it many correct solution paths.

paras: The paper swaps the model's output at each reasoning step. Normally the model outputs a single word (a one-hot distribution: 100% to one word, 0% to all others). Instead, it outputs a soft blend (a mixture: different fractions spread across many words). That soft token (a set of numbers representing the blended words) becomes the input to the next step.
object.object: Output from single word to soft blend

hidden.h2: Tracking parallelism: how many paths at once
hidden.name: Parallelism capacity
paras: The paper measures a quantity called parallelism: how many different reasoning branches can the model hold in the soft tokens at once? A soft token at step 2 can represent multiple paths from step 1 only if the model has enough embedding dimension (the number of numbers used to represent each word). If the dimension is too small, the soft blends start to crush and mix together, and paths interfere.

The paper proves mathematically that the embedding dimension directly controls the maximum parallelism. More dimensions mean more branches. They show that a one-layer transformer (a simple model that reads inputs and produces outputs in one pass) with sine and cosine embeddings can pack all possible states of a search problem (like exploring all subsets in the subset-sum problem) if the dimension is large enough.

heat.caption: Darker dimension means more branches; at dim 24 the model starts solving hard problems without confusion.

reads.html: The embedding dimension is how many numbers describe each soft token. Bigger numbers give the model more room to hold separate branches.
The paper proves that a transformer with sine and cosine embeddings can store all reachable states if dimension d is at least 2^k, where k is the number of branches at that step.

paras: The key is that soft tokens preserve superposition: when you blend word A, word B, and word C into one token, that token retains information about all three. The model's attention layer (the part that decides which earlier word to read) can read from all three branches at once. Each path flows forward on its own, like water splitting through channels and then joining at the end.

During training, the model learns which soft blend to output at each step by matching target distributions. Instead of teaching it to output word A with probability 100%, the paper shows the model many correct solution paths and teaches it to output the weighted average of all correct next steps. This grounds the soft tokens in real problem-solving strategies.

At inference, the model samples a handful of words (say, 5 words) from the soft blend and averages their embeddings (the numerical representations). This discrete sampling keeps the soft token well-defined while still holding multiple paths. The model then feeds this averaged embedding forward, and the next step can branch again.

stages.s: Multiple reasoning paths all mixed into one soft token
Attention reads across all branches in the blend
Each path evolves; output is the next soft blend
Final answer picks the best branch

math.words: Minimize the difference between what the model outputs and the blended distribution of all target traces at each step.
math.equation: Loss = sum over steps t of divergence(output_distribution_t, target_blend_t)
symbols: The soft token the model produces at step t (fractions summing to 1)
The average of target distributions at step t across all correct paths
A measure of how different two distributions are (like distance between them)
Add up the error at every reasoning step

worked.title: Tiny worked example: learning to blend two paths
lines: Suppose at step 2, path A says the next word is apple (100%), and path B says banana (100%).
The target blend at step 2 is: 50% apple, 50% banana.
Divergence measures how far 60%/40% is from 50%/50%.
Loss = that divergence (plus losses from all other steps).

math.note: The model learns the right soft blend by watching many successful reasoning paths and averaging their next-word choices.

charts.title: Discrete one-word model
charts.note: Model gets stuck because it cannot hold multiple branches at once. Needs more layers to recover.

charts.title: Continuous soft-blend model
charts.note: Model holds all branches in soft tokens. One layer with large dimension solves the problem cleanly.

items.html: If the model does not have enough embedding capacity, different branches start to crush and interfere. The soft token becomes gibberish and paths mix together. The model needs dimension to scale with the number of branches.

items.b: Sampling too few words from the blend.
items.html: If you sample only 1 word instead of 5 or more, the soft token collapses back to discrete. You lose the parallelism benefit.
The supervision depends on having good example solutions to learn from. If all target paths are suboptimal, the model learns to blend garbage.
With enough embedding dimension, diverse target paths, and K-token sampling, the soft tokens preserve branch separation and solve reasoning problems efficiently.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small transformer and train it on the subset-sum problem: given a list of numbers (like 3, 7, 2, 5, 9), find the subset that sums to a target value (say, 15). This is a search problem where the model must explore multiple branches. Train one version with discrete (one-word) outputs and one with continuous (soft-blend) outputs. Both should use the same embedding dimension. Measure how many steps each needs and how often they find the right answer.
demo.metric_eq: Success rate = (times model found correct subset sum) / (total test cases)
demo.closing: The soft-blend model should find the answer with far fewer steps and higher accuracy because it holds multiple branches. The discrete model should get stuck on hard cases.
